entities.summary: Gaius Porcius Cato was a Roman politician and general, who served as consul in 114 BC, playing a crucial role in shaping the late Roman Republic. Born into a prominent family, Cato was the son of Marcus Porcius Cato Licinianus and grandson of Cato the Censor, a renowned statesman. He rose to prominence as a champion of the aristocracy, advocating for the restoration of the Roman Republic's original constitution and the expulsion of the Roman king. Cato's leadership and influence led to the formation of the First Triumvirate, a powerful alliance between himself, Julius Caesar, and Pompey the Great. This alliance ultimately led to Cato's downfall, as he became increasingly at odds with Caesar's growing power. Cato's legacy extends beyond his political career, as he was a patron of the arts and a prolific writer, leaving behind a body of work that includes his treatise on agriculture, De Agri Cultura. Despite his passing in 160 BCE, Cato's impact on Roman politics and society continues to be felt, with his commitment to the principles of liberty and the rule of law remaining a cornerstone of Western democratic values.
